strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing real gap between LLM-generated molecules and synthesis feasibility
Sensible technical approach using functional building blocks as tokens with clear analogy to word-level NLP tokenization
Thoughtful incorporation of synthesis constraints through synthesis-guaranteed tokenizer limited to three automated reactions
Comprehensive data preparation including synthetic data generation and activity cliffs for contrastive learning
Multimodal bilingual model design combining natural language and molecular representations via code-switching
Clear, well-written presentation with compelling real-world case studies (fallen angels: Evobrutinib, TNG348)
Large-scale pretraining on diverse datasets and testing on 430 FDA-approved drugs
weaknesses: No experimental validation of central synthesis feasibility claim—no wet lab synthesis, retrosynthetic analysis, or comparison of synthesis difficulty vs. baselines
Missing baseline comparisons to SMILES-based optimization, graph-based generation, genetic algorithms, or other LLM approaches
Weak evaluation: only 6 ADMET properties, modest inconsistent improvements (PGP degrades), small effect sizes, no ablation studies
Potential data leakage: model trained on SMolInstruct/Mol-Instructions; overlap with evaluation set unclear
Circular evaluation: oracle ADMET models trained on TDC then used to evaluate molecules optimized on same properties
Limited scope: only 430 molecules, primarily modifications of existing drugs rather than diverse chemistry; only 2 case studies
Algorithm 1 vague: unclear whether iterative refinement uses oracle models or model-based reasoning
Synthesis constraint limited: only 3 reaction types; ignores protecting groups, selectivity, functional group compatibility, starting material availability
Questionable generalization claims: 426/430 FDA drugs contain unseen blocks; this raises questions rather than demonstrating understanding
Reproducibility concerns: no code availability, complex multi-stage training, full finetuning required, many hyperparameters
Missing ablations: no validation of design choices (necessity of bilingual training, GNN encoding contribution, impact of vocabulary size)
Incomplete analysis: no error analysis, no evaluation of molecular types that cannot be represented, no trade-off analysis for multi-objective optimization
Architecture novelty limited: standard Transformer decoder + GNN encoder; main contribution is tokenization strategy and training setup

strengths: Well-motivated problem: addresses important gap between AI-generated molecules and practical synthesizability
Conceptually sound approach grounded in medicinal chemistry practice (building blocks vs atoms)
Comprehensive data construction effort including synthetic data via activity cliffs and oracle ensembles
Practical focus on real FDA drugs and clinical failures demonstrates real-world engagement
weaknesses: Critical flaw: No baseline comparisons to any existing methods (MolT5, GIMLET, SMILES-based models). Claims of improvement are meaningless without baselines
Circular evaluation: Oracle models used for both synthetic label generation and evaluation creates overfitting risk and invalidates claims
Weak experimental validation: Small test set (430 drugs, 2 anecdotal examples); improvements are modest (5-10 points); unvalidated synthesizability claims
Unclear methodology: Algorithm 1 vague on inference; 'chemical reasoning' appears to be oracle-guided search; two-stage tokenization is ad-hoc with unknown failure rates
Limited architectural novelty: Standard transformer + GNN concatenation; main contribution is conceptual, not technical
Missing critical experiments: No ablations, no retrosynthesis validation, no expert review of proposed molecules, no systematic analysis of learned patterns
Reproducibility concerns: Complex multi-stage training with ad-hoc choices (separate loss heads, frozen/unfrozen components, 1000-token filtering); difficult to reproduce
Overstated claims: 'Guarantees synthesis-friendly molecules' unvalidated; 'significantly improving' applied to modest improvements where one metric worsened
Limited scope: Only 6 ADMET properties, 1000 blocks, no novel chemical space evaluation, no analysis of what model learns
Data and evaluation issues: Oracle models show AUC <0.85 for some tasks; activity cliff construction may miss SAR patterns; test set may contaminate with pretraining data

strengths: Novel and well-motivated core idea: tokenizing molecules at the functional building block level for synthesis compatibility addresses a genuine gap in existing molecular generation models
Practical problem formulation: tackles the real issue of LLMs generating non-synthesizable molecules
Comprehensive technical approach: thoughtful dual tokenization strategy (synthesis-guaranteed + rule-based), natural language integration, and multi-objective optimization capability
Impressive data infrastructure: large-scale pretraining effort with diverse sources and careful synthetic data generation using activity cliffs
Creative experimental design: 'fallen angels' case study demonstrates practical relevance; out-of-vocabulary generalization evaluation shows robustness
Clear presentation and effective visualizations, particularly Figures 1-3 which illustrate key concepts well
weaknesses: Critically missing baseline comparisons: no quantitative evaluation against MolT5, GIMLET, DrugAssist, or other molecular generation/optimization methods makes it impossible to assess if improvements come from the tokenization strategy vs. synthetic data or oracle models
Unvalidated core claims: synthesizability guarantee relies only on tokenization logic; no wet-lab validation, retrosynthesis analysis, or comparison to other methods' synthesizability
Absent ablation studies: no evaluation of individual contributions from dual tokenization, natural language components, or vocabulary size choices

Modest improvements with unclear significance: Table 1 shows small changes (AMES 59.5→54.0, PGP 66.0→68.0), no actual p-values reported, and one property degrades (PGP) despite being marked for improvement
Heavy oracle model dependency: improvements depend critically on ensemble model quality and potential biases; no error analysis or sensitivity to oracle performance
Methodological concerns: activity cliff definition arbitrary (Murcko scaffolds) without sensitivity analysis; oracle error propagation through training data not analyzed
Incomplete experimental analysis: no coverage statistics for synthesis-guaranteed tokenizer, no sensitivity analyses, complex training procedure (staged, separated losses) lacks justification
Limited model architecture novelty: standard Transformer decoder; main contribution is tokenization and data preparation rather than modeling innovations
Reproducibility issues: no code availability mentioned, heavy data filtering, many hyperparameter choices unexplained, oracle model details relegated to appendix
Scalability and deployment concerns: requires 20GB VRAM, restricted to 1000 blocks, no inference efficiency analysis

strengths: Novel synthesis-aware tokenization at building block level with clear motivation and practical grounding in chemistry
Rigorous synthesizability evaluation showing 100% validity and 98.23% makeability using Allchemy, substantially outperforming baselines
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across 122 FDA-approved drugs with 8 baseline comparisons and extensive supplementary documentation
Well-designed synthesis-guaranteed tokenizer that ensures generated molecules compatible with automated synthesis platforms (3 reaction types)
Multimodal bilingual approach combining natural language and molecular representations is well-motivated and technically sound
Strong commitment to reproducibility with promised release of code, data, models, and extensive methodological details
weaknesses: Modest empirical improvements (15% average on ADMET properties) without statistical significance testing or confidence intervals
Severe vocabulary limitations with only 1,000 blocks; restricted out-of-distribution testing (122 molecules, 153 unseen blocks) raises generalization concerns
Reliance on oracle models (AUCs 0.84-0.99) for ADMET labels without quantifying distribution shift or error propagation to training data
Complete absence of experimental wet-lab validation; 'fallen angels' case study with only 2 molecules is speculative without synthesis/bioassay
Limited architectural novelty; core contribution is tokenization and training data design rather than model innovation; no ablations comparing tokenizer variants
Restricted chemical diversity due to 3-reaction constraint; only 26.7% of FDA corpus covered by synthesis-guaranteed tokenizer; applicability beyond drug discovery underdeveloped
Small sample sizes for key evaluations (200 molecules for Allchemy); no error bars, confidence intervals, or variance analysis across random seeds
Design choice to separate molecule/language classifier heads lacks justification and impact analysis; Algorithm 1 for property selection is vague
High computational requirements (4× A100-80GB GPUs) create reproducibility barrier; GNN pre-training adds complexity

strengths: Well-motivated core idea of using synthesis-friendly building blocks as tokens, elegantly addressing the synthesizability gap of existing generative models
Grounded in real chemistry with clear connection to automated block-based synthesis platforms and established chemistry (amide coupling, Suzuki-Miyaura, Buchwald-Hartwig)
Comprehensive experimental framework including large-scale dataset (36M instructions), proper oracle ensemble modeling, and rigorous synthesizability evaluation using Allchemy
Strong empirical results on defined metrics: 15% property improvement, 100% validity vs 93.8% baseline, 98.2% synthesizability, outperforms GPT-5/Gemini
Thoughtful multimodal architecture elegantly blending molecular graphs and natural language via code-switching approach
Extensive documentation and reproducibility attention with detailed appendices covering tokenization, hyperparameters, and data sources
weaknesses: No experimental validation: all claims are purely computational (oracle predictions, SA scores, Allchemy retrosynthesis). No wet lab synthesis or measured bioassay values provided, undermining core claims about real synthesizability and property improvements
Weak evaluation set: only 122 FDA drugs with synthesis-guaranteed blocks; test set too small for strong conclusions. Only 200 molecules evaluated with expensive Allchemy tool

Oracle model dependence: all property improvements predicted by ensemble models (≤0.99 AUC) rather than measured data. These biases could systematically favor mCLM outputs. No measured bioassays from ChEMBL

Problematic vocabulary coverage: only 26.7% of full dataset tokenizable with strict synthesis-guaranteed rules; remainder uses fallback rule-based tokenizer during training, undermining synthesizability guarantees claim

Unfair baseline comparisons: all baselines (GPT-4o, MoleculeSTM, Gemini) are unconstrained methods not designed for synthesis-guaranteed generation. No comparison to synthesis-aware baselines makes synthesizability advantage somewhat circular

Missing critical ablations: no study of GNN contribution, multimodal vs text-only, or direct comparison of synthesis-guaranteed vs rule-based tokenization on same molecules. Cannot isolate key design choices

Overstated claims on multi-objective reasoning: Algorithm 1 is simple greedy iteration, not principled Pareto optimization. Only 2 cherry-picked 'fallen angel' examples shown with no systematic validation. Claims like 'rescue' are inflated for computational predictions
Limited architectural novelty: core model (Transformer + GNN + adapter) is straightforward; main novelty is tokenization/dataset construction, not modeling innovation

Dataset construction concerns: heavy oracle-model dependence for label generation, activity-cliff training data is subset not representative of all chemistry, complex pipeline difficult to reproduce without released code
Scope limitations: evaluated only on 6 ADMET properties for drug-like molecules; OPV materials relegated to appendix; by design confined to ~1000 known blocks so cannot explore truly novel chemistry

strengths: Novel building block-level tokenization approach well-motivated by natural language processing and protein LLM analogies, directly addressing the atom-level tokenization limitations
Genuine practical contribution through synthesis-guaranteed design using three automated reactions, enabling seamless transition from in silico to real-world synthesis
Comprehensive and rigorous evaluation with strong baselines (GPT-4o, GPT-5, Gemini, Claude, MoleculeSTM) and novel assessment using state-of-the-art Allchemy retrosynthesis software
Impressive empirical results: 100% validity, 98.23% synthesizability (exceeding FDA drugs at 98.11%), and 15% average property improvement across ADMET properties
Well-designed multimodal integration combining natural language descriptions with molecular building blocks through elegant GNN-LLM architecture
Substantial data engineering effort (36M molecular instructions, 8M molecules, activity cliff mining, oracle ensemble) that advances the field infrastructure
Practical demonstrations through fallen angels case study showing iterative multi-objective optimization on real clinical candidates (Evobrutinib, TNG348)
Excellent reproducibility provisions: detailed appendices on training, tokenization, data construction, and commitment to release code/data
Modular tokenizer design enabling straightforward incorporation of new automated reactions as they're validated in practice
weaknesses: Severely limited vocabulary: only 1,000 building blocks from ~800k available; lacks analysis of chemical space coverage and generalization to novel scaffolds—a fundamental constraint on applicability

Core synthesizability claims lack experimental validation: all results are computational (Allchemy-based) on small sample (200 molecules); no wet-lab synthesis validation despite this being the central claim

Circular dependency on oracle models for training data: ADMET oracles achieve 0.80-0.99 AUC on TDC but generalization to novel molecules unvalidated; error propagation not analyzed; results are improvements relative to oracles, not ground truth
Limited out-of-distribution evaluation: 120/122 FDA drugs contain unseen blocks but remain 98% in-distribution; no evaluation on truly novel chemical series weakens generalization claims

Tokenization reaction constraints create fundamental trade-off: restricting to three automated reactions excludes useful transformations, systematically biases chemical space, and reduces diversity compared to atom-level approaches—inadequately discussed

Multi-objective optimization incomplete: acknowledged as central to drug discovery but critical chemical reasoning only handles sequential single-property optimization; fallen angels example optimizes sequentially, not simultaneously
Weak chemistry-specific baselines: main comparison is MoleculeSTM (2022); general LLMs (GPT-4o/5, Claude) aren't chemistry-focused; missing recent specialized molecule generation methods
Insufficient ablation studies: no ablation on multimodal vs. molecule-only, reaction type contributions, or GNN necessity; unclear whether architectural choices are optimal
Potential data contamination: FDA drugs appear in training instruction datasets; while exact molecules excluded from tests, similar scaffolds in training could inflate FDA drug evaluation results
Molecule token learning difficulties inadequately addressed: 10x loss difference between molecule and text tokens suggests architectural issues; GNN frozen during most training limits learning

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing the real gap between in silico generation and practical synthesizability
Technically sound dual-tokenization strategy with synthesis-guaranteed and rule-based fallback mechanisms
Rigorous experimental validation including Allchemy retrosynthesis on supercomputing cluster (200 molecules per model)
Impressive synthesizability metrics: 100% validity and 98.2% makeability vs. 84.8% for MoleculeSTM baseline
Comprehensive baseline comparisons including GPT-4o/5, Gemini, Claude, and relevant molecular generation methods
Strong ablation studies demonstrating importance of GNN (22.5% drop without) and tokenizer choice (34% drop)
Out-of-vocabulary generalization test: 120/122 FDA drugs contain unseen building blocks
Large-scale dataset with 8M molecules, 800k building blocks, and 36M+ instructions with thoughtful synthetic data generation using activity cliffs
Compelling 'fallen angels' case study demonstrating iterative multi-step refinement on clinically failed drugs
Excellent presentation, clear motivation, and comprehensive reproducibility details (31-page appendix)
weaknesses: Incremental novelty: building-block tokenization similar to GroupSELFIES, SAFE, and contemporary Reasyn; limited distinction from prior work on why GNN encoding is fundamentally superior
Critical vocabulary bottleneck: model trained on only 1,000 blocks (0.125% of 800k available); no empirical demonstration of scaling to larger vocabularies despite claims of compatibility
Very limited evaluation scope: only 122 synthesis-guaranteed FDA drugs and 6 ADMET properties; no evaluation on diverse chemical space or standard benchmarks (GUACAMOL)
Modest improvements over strongest baseline: 15.0% vs. Gemini's 6.98% (only ~8% advantage); improvements vs. MoleculeSTM are larger but baseline not optimized for task
Training misalignment: molecule tokens learn 10× slower than text tokens, requiring separate classifier heads—indicates imperfect multimodal fusion and necessity of architectural workarounds
Oracle model dependency: ADMET predictions rely on ensemble models with AUC 0.80-0.99 introducing potential out-of-distribution errors; Allchemy validation limited to 200 sampled molecules

Coverage limitations: only 26.7% of compounds fully tokenizable with synthesis guarantees; 73.3% require fallback rule-based tokenizer without guarantees, diluting 'guaranteed synthesizability' claims

Overclaimed reasoning: 'critical chemical reasoning' is essentially greedy sequential single-property optimization; no comparison with sophisticated multi-objective methods (Pareto, MOEA/D); fallen angels show mixed success
No experimental validation: no physical synthesis or lab validation of proposed molecules; no runtime/inference cost analysis; no failure case analysis
Statistical rigor: no confidence intervals or significance testing; small test set (122 drugs) lacks power; no ablation on separate vs. unified heads for molecule/text streams

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing the gap between in-silico generation and practical synthesizability
Novel synthesis-aware tokenization based on automation-friendly reactions (Buchwald-Hartwig, Suzuki-Miyaura, amide coupling)
Strong synthesizability results: 100% validity and 98.23% synthesizability verified via state-of-the-art Allchemy retrosynthesis tool
Large-scale multimodal dataset construction (36M instructions, 8M molecules) with careful property-based synthetic data generation
Rigorous evaluation with extensive baselines (GPT-4o/5, Gemini, Claude, MoleculeSTM) and oracle models achieving >0.89 AUC on ADMET tasks
Practical case study on 'fallen angels' (drugs that failed clinical trials) demonstrates potential real-world applications
weaknesses: Property optimization results are weak: 15% average improvement is modest with inconsistent gains (HIA: 98.96→98.99, PGP: 64.6→64.4, suspicious BBBP jump 61.4→85.2 suggesting oracle bias)
Critical dependence on oracle models without uncertainty quantification; oracle predictions used as training targets may propagate errors; data leakage risk from oracle training on TDC

Artificial evaluation constraints: uses only 1,000 of 200k available blocks (justified only by computational cost), evaluates on just 122 OOD molecules and 6 ADMET properties, primarily tests on already-optimized FDA drugs
No experimental validation: all results are computational; despite claiming 'makeable molecules,' provides no wet-lab synthesis evidence; Allchemy predictions not validated experimentally

Circular advantage in synthesizability: constraining to synthesis-friendly blocks makes high synthesizability a construction artifact; ablation shows 73.65% without synthesis tokenizer, raising question of model vs. constraint contribution
Limited architectural novelty: core model is standard Qwen2.5-3B with conventional GNN adapters (LLaVA-style); main contribution is tokenization scheme and training data, not method innovation

Incomplete multi-objective optimization: Algorithm 1 improves properties sequentially rather than jointly; drug discovery is inherently multi-objective but this isn't addressed; 'fallen angels' shows only 2 anecdotal examples
Weak baseline comparisons: MoleculeSTM (2022) and FineMolTex are not strong chemistry baselines; GPT models are general-purpose and unfair comparisons; missing recent specialized chemistry models
Reproducibility concerns: promised data not provided for review; oracle training details scattered; generation hyperparameters missing; questionable Zipf's law justification for 800k→1k filtering

Limited and insufficient ablations: only GNN and tokenizer variants tested; missing ablations on reaction types, vocabulary sizes, GNN architecture; Llama vs. Qwen shows 15% vs. 2.82% gap but unexplored
Coverage-synthesizability trade-off unexplored: only 26.7% use synthesis-guaranteed tokenizer, 73.3% use rule-based fallback; fallback is an 'escape hatch' that weakens guarantees
'Fallen angels' analysis lacks rigor: only 2 drug examples; no independent validation of proposed improvements; no expert chemist evaluation; claimed similarity to prior work is speculative
Narrow evaluation scope: dominated by drug discovery; OPV materials minimally evaluated; unclear generalization beyond ADMET properties
Statistical issues: 'average improvement' metric unclear (how combine lower/higher-is-better?); no confidence intervals or significance testing; improvement percentages calculated inconsistently

strengths: Novel and well-motivated core contribution: Tokenizing molecules at the level of synthesis-friendly building blocks elegantly addresses the gap between in-silico generation and laboratory practice, with compelling analogy to word-level tokenization in NLP

Synthesizability as a first-class constraint: Unlike prior work adding synthesizability post-hoc, mCLM guarantees 100% validity and 98.23% synthesizability by design, matching FDA drugs and substantially exceeding baselines (MoleculeSTM: 84.8%)

Rigorous and comprehensive evaluation: Strong baseline comparisons (GPT-4o, GPT-5, Gemini), validation using Allchemy retrosynthesis software with documented lab pedigree, multiple complementary metrics, and testing on 122 FDA drugs with 153 unseen building blocks

Significant empirical results: 15% average improvement in ADMET properties substantially exceeds GPT-5 (-0.82%) despite using only 3B parameters, demonstrating that synthesis-friendly tokenization improves both synthesizability and functionality

Excellent reproducibility: Extensive appendices with detailed tokenizer algorithms, training procedures, hyperparameters, oracle model construction, ablations, and commitment to release code and data upon publication

Elegant multimodal integration: The 'code-switching' approach seamlessly blends GNN-encoded molecular structures with natural language descriptions using a unified loss function and shared embedding space

Practical case studies: The 'fallen angels' examples (Evobrutinib, TNG348) demonstrate iterative multi-objective refinement and identify chemical modifications that align with independent literature findings (Maji et al., 2023)

Large-scale data engineering: Curation of 36 million molecular instructions from 8 million molecules with sophisticated synthetic data generation via activity cliffs and oracle ensembles demonstrates serious engineering effort
weaknesses: Vocabulary scale severely constrained: Training uses only 1,000 of 800k available building blocks (0.125% coverage) due to computational limitations. No demonstration of scaling to larger vocabularies (10k, 100k), limiting coverage of chemical space and generalizability claims

Lack of real-world synthesis validation: All synthesizability claims rest on computational validation via Allchemy software. No wet-lab synthesis of generated molecules reported. The cited Allchemy validation refers to its own dataset, not mCLM outputs

Constrained evaluation domain: Evaluation limited to FDA-approved drugs and 6 ADMET properties. No testing on truly novel chemical structures or other critical properties (binding affinity, cell permeability, metabolism). Generalization to unexplored chemical space unclear

Oracle model quality concerns: ADMET predictions from ensemble models (AUC: 0.84-0.99) rather than experimental data. Oracles trained on fixed benchmarks with likely distribution mismatch for novel molecules. Model optimizes oracle predictions, not actual properties

Limited statistical rigor: No error bars, confidence intervals, or statistical significance tests in main results. Only 200 molecules sampled per baseline for Allchemy evaluation. Unclear if improvements are statistically significant or reproducible

Multi-objective optimization poorly addressed: Algorithm 1 is simplistic (iteratively select worst property and regenerate). Authors acknowledge other properties may be compromised. Only 2 case studies shown; scalability to >6 properties unclear. No formal convergence analysis or Pareto optimization

Computational cost not reported: Training on 4× A100 GPUs mentioned but no total compute budget, inference time comparisons, or memory footprint discussion. Hard to assess practical utility relative to baselines

Limited failure analysis and ablation studies: No investigation of failure modes, underutilized building blocks, or which molecule classes underperform. No ablation on contributions of different data sources (SMolInstruct vs. oracle data). Severe performance degradation in No GNN ablation (-7.53%) not explained

Incomplete baseline comparisons: While comprehensive, comparisons with GPT-4o/GPT-5 are somewhat unfair since these are general-purpose models. Relevant domain-specific baselines somewhat dated. Recent work like Reasyn mentioned but not compared

Missing critical experiments: No scaling studies with different vocabulary sizes, no evaluation on non-ADMET properties, no de novo generation of truly novel molecules, no synthesis validation experiments, no analysis of how oracle quality affects downstream performance
